say: So. You've got a few clankers running, and you're tokenmaxxing like everyone else.
To get anything done, they need to work in parallel, each on its own branch.
But in one checkout, they clash. One switches branches under another, and your login fix lands on another agent's branch.
Duuuh. I'm not a caveman, you say. Git has worktrees for this. A fresh worktree, in about a second.
But it starts empty. No dependencies, no dev shell, none of your local files. Just vibes.

So your agent improvises. It reinstalls everything in every worktree. Or it gives up: it can't lint here, can't regenerate the protos here, so it reaches back into your main checkout and links things across.
And the next agent rediscovers all of it, from scratch, every single time.
On a big monorepo, that's over a minute and gigabytes of disk, per worktree. Your laptop fan has opinions.
But there's a better way. Meet clove.
clove keeps one golden image of your repo, with dependencies installed and the environment warmed. Each worktree is a copy-on-write clone of it.
It detects your toolchain on its own: mise, direnv and nix, pnpm, bun, yarn, npm, uv and cargo, plus your local files. Anything else is a step in a small config file, shared with your team.
And it stays warm on its own. Each time you pull, a background service refreshes the golden image, while your clones keep working.

Under the hood, it leans on what your file system already does well. On macOS, each clone is an APFS disk image, copied whole by a single clonefile call. On Linux, it's a btrfs snapshot, taken in a few milliseconds.
So a new worktree is ready in about a second. Everything is already there, and your fan and your disk can finally relax.
When a lockfile changes, only that step runs again.
Use it from the command line, from a full-screen terminal interface, or from the desktop app, on macOS and Linux.
It brings your clones up to date, with Claude resolving the conflicts. It cleans up after merged pull requests. And it teaches your agents to use it, so you don't have to.
That's clove. Your worktrees, ready in a second.
